sections.title: What you already know
sections.content: You know *cuyo*, *cuya*, *cuyos* and *cuyas* from B1 Unit 5. They join two clauses and mean "whose": *un imperio cuya capital era Cuzco*. They agree with the thing owned (*capital* is feminine, so *cuya*), not with the owner.

items.spanish: El imperio inca tenía una capital: Cuzco. → Era un imperio cuya capital era Cuzco.
items.english: The Inca empire had a capital, Cuzco. → It was an empire whose capital was Cuzco.

items.spanish: Los chasquis eran mensajeros cuyo trabajo era llevar noticias.
items.english: The chasquis were messengers whose job was to carry news.

items.spanish: Machu Picchu, cuyos muros de piedra se construyeron en el siglo XV, está en las montañas.
items.english: Machu Picchu, whose stone walls were built in the fifteenth century, is in the mountains.

items.spanish: Los incas construyeron una red de caminos cuyo conjunto fue declarado Patrimonio Mundial.
items.english: The Incas built a network of roads whose whole was declared a World Heritage Site.

sections.content: *Cuyo* is never followed by an article: *cuya capital*, not *cuya la capital*. It always sits between the owner and the thing owned (*imperio cuya capital*). If you can say "whose" in English, think of *cuyo*.
